Chide

/CHYDE/ - rhymes with ride · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Chide means to scold gently; to voice mild disapproval.

The yoga teacher chided us for rushing the cooldown — one raised eyebrow and a soft 'again, slowly.'

Worked Example

When the new hire signed his emails with just his initials, the office manager chided him in passing: 'We do full names here, friend.'

Chide is the gentlest word on the scolding shelf: mild disapproval voiced without anger, often with warmth still in it. If voices rise or the correction goes on the record, you have left chide behind for its sterner cousins.

How Strong Is It? — tease → chide → scold

tease vs. chide

tease vs. chide: Teasing is play, not correction — even gentler than chide, which does mean the disapproval.

scold vs. chide

scold vs. chide: Scold goes further than chide: real anger in the voice, where chide keeps its warmth.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — chide

Root — chide: to quarrel, scold (Old English cidan)

Put it together

Put it together: Chide is a single Old English word, cidan, 'to quarrel or scold,' worn smooth by a thousand years of use. There is nothing to peel off here — no prefix, no suffix, no borrowed root: plain homegrown scolding, which may be why it sounds so gentle.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old English cidan left no other descendants: chide is its entire surviving family. Words that stayed home in English often come to us short, blunt, and single — unlike the Latin scolding words built from parts, like admonish and chastise on this unit's other cards.

Strength Check

Word Choice

gentle / conversational

Chide is scolding with the affection left in — for grandmothers, coaches, and old friends. If real anger enters, you have moved to admonish or berate (this unit); if there is no disapproval at all, it was only teasing.
